introduction-why-processes-need-to-talk.core: Processes are isolated: separate address spaces, so they can't read each other's memory. Yet systems are built from cooperating processes (web server and app server, a database and its workers, shells and pipelines). IPC mechanisms trade speed, simplicity and structure: pipes for streams, signals for notifications, Unix sockets for local client/server, shared memory and mmap for zero-copy bulk data, and message queues and TCP for structured or networked communication.

first_principles.problem: A team uses TCP loopback for a high-frequency local cache and wonders why latency is higher than expected.
truths: Copies and context switches cost time.
derivation: Use **pipes** for streams between related processes.

analogy.title: Ways neighbours communicate
analogy.story: Passing notes under the door (pipes), knocking (signals), an intercom (sockets), or a shared noticeboard (shared memory).
analogy.breaks: Neighbours share language; processes need agreed formats and synchronisation.

example.title: Choosing
flow: Video frames between processes → shared memory

check.q: Why do processes need IPC mechanisms at all?
check.a: Each has its own isolated address space, so they can't directly access each other's memory without kernel-provided channels.

pipes-and-named-pipes-fifos.core: A pipe is a one-way kernel buffer (64 KB by default on Linux) with a write end and a read end, typically created by the shell between related processes (ls | grep). Writers block when it's full and readers block when it's empty, giving natural backpressure; when all writers close, readers see EOF, and writing to a pipe with no reader raises SIGPIPE. Named pipes (FIFOs, via mkfifo) appear in the filesystem so unrelated processes can connect.

first_principles.problem: A pipeline hangs because the consumer stops reading and the producer blocks on a full pipe buffer.

analogy.title: A pneumatic tube with limited capacity
analogy.story: Messages go one way; if the receiver doesn't empty it, the sender has to wait.
analogy.breaks: Tubes are physical; pipe capacity is configurable up to pipe-max-size.

code.text:
mkfifo /tmp/events
( while read line; do echo "got: $line"; done < /tmp/events ) &
echo 'deploy finished' > /tmp/events
# yes | head -1   → 'yes' gets SIGPIPE when head exits

check.q: What happens when a process writes to a pipe whose reader has exited?
check.a: It receives SIGPIPE (or EPIPE if the signal is ignored).

signals-the-lightweight-notification-cha.core: Signals are asynchronous notifications carrying just a number: SIGTERM, SIGHUP, SIGUSR1/2, SIGCHLD, SIGINT. The kernel interrupts the target process to run its handler or default action. They're good for simple events (reload, shutdown, child exited) but carry no data (beyond siginfo), can coalesce (multiple pending of the same type merge into one), and handlers are restricted to async-signal-safe functions. Use signalfd or the self-pipe trick in event loops.

first_principles.problem: A signal handler that logs with printf and takes a mutex occasionally deadlocks the process.

analogy.title: A doorbell with no message
analogy.story: It tells you someone's there but not why, and two quick rings can sound like one.
analogy.breaks: Doorbells don't interrupt you mid-sentence; signals interrupt mid-instruction.

check.q: Why should signal handlers only set a flag?
check.a: Signals can interrupt any code, so calling non-reentrant functions (printf, malloc, locks) in handlers risks deadlocks or corruption.

unix-domain-sockets-uds-vs-tcp-loopback.core: Unix domain sockets use the socket API but stay inside the kernel, with no TCP/IP stack, checksums, congestion control or port allocation, so they have lower latency and higher throughput than TCP over 127.0.0.1. They live as filesystem paths (permissions give access control) or abstract names, support stream and datagram modes, pass file descriptors between processes (SCM_RIGHTS), and report peer credentials (SO_PEERCRED). Databases, Docker and systemd use them heavily.

first_principles.problem: An app talks to a local Redis over TCP localhost at 30% higher latency than necessary.

analogy.title: An internal mail tube vs posting a letter to yourself
analogy.story: Both arrive, but the internal tube skips the post office entirely.
analogy.breaks: Mail tubes carry paper; UDS can even pass open file handles.

code.text:
# redis.conf
# unixsocket /run/redis/redis.sock
# unixsocketperm 770
redis-benchmark -s /run/redis/redis.sock -t get -n 1000000 -q
redis-benchmark -h 127.0.0.1 -t get -n 1000000 -q
# GET: ~180k rps (UDS) vs ~130k rps (TCP loopback)

check.q: Why are Unix domain sockets faster than TCP loopback?
check.a: They bypass the TCP/IP stack (checksums, congestion control, packet processing) and copy data directly between sockets in the kernel.

shared-memory-the-zero-copy-fast-path.core: Shared memory maps the same physical pages into several processes, via POSIX shm_open plus mmap, System V shmget, or memfd_create, so data written by one is instantly visible to the other with no kernel copies. It's the fastest IPC, used by databases (PostgreSQL shared buffers), browsers and video pipelines, but you must synchronise yourself (futexes, semaphores, lock-free ring buffers with atomics and memory barriers) and handle crash cleanup.

first_principles.problem: Copying 4K video frames through sockets between processes uses 30% CPU.
truths: Same pages can map into many processes.

analogy.title: A shared whiteboard between offices
analogy.story: Everyone sees updates instantly with no memos, but you need rules about who writes when.
analogy.breaks: Whiteboards are visible to all; shared memory needs explicit memory barriers for visibility ordering.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Frames shared with no copies; CPU drops sharply.

check.q: What's the main burden of using shared memory for IPC?
check.a: You must implement synchronisation and memory ordering yourself (locks, atomics, barriers) and handle cleanup.

mmap-files-masquerading-as-memory.core: mmap maps a file (or anonymous memory) into a process's address space. Reads and writes become memory accesses, with pages loaded lazily via page faults and written back by the kernel (or msync). It avoids read() copies, lets the page cache be shared between processes, and suits random access to large files. The pitfalls are page-fault latency, SIGBUS if a file shrinks, unpredictable I/O timing, and limited control over flushing, which is why some databases avoid it.

first_principles.problem: A search index uses read() into buffers, doubling memory use with page cache plus user copies.
truths: The page cache already holds file data.
derivation: **mmap** file with PROT_READ (and MAP_SHARED to write).

analogy.title: Reading a library book on the shelf vs photocopying it
analogy.story: Instead of copying pages to your desk, you read directly from the shelf, and others can read the same copy.
analogy.breaks: Books don't change size; truncated files cause SIGBUS.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Memory use halved; page cache shared.

code.text:
import mmap, os
fd = os.open("index.bin", os.O_RDONLY)
with mmap.mmap(fd, 0, prot=mmap.PROT_READ) as m:
    m.madvise(mmap.MADV_RANDOM)
    header = m[:64]           # page fault loads only touched pages
    entry = m[off:off + 128]

check.q: What causes SIGBUS when using mmap on a file?
check.a: Accessing a mapped page beyond the file's current end, e.g. after the file was truncated by another process.
